cards.front: How has biodiversity changed over the history of life on Earth?
cards.back: Overall it has **risen** over hundreds of millions of years, but not steadily. Sudden falls during mass extinctions were followed by recovery as survivors gave rise to new species.

cards.front: How can fossils show changes in biodiversity through time?
cards.back: Counting the fossil types in each dated rock layer shows diversity. A **sudden fall** marks an extinction event, and later layers show recovery.
cards.hint: Think about what you count in each layer.

cards.front: Why does a cause such as habitat loss lead to extinction?
cards.back: Each cause cuts a species’ **survival or reproduction** until too few individuals remain to keep the species going.
cards.hint: Follow the effect on individuals and their numbers.

cards.back: **Biodiversity** is variation within species, between species, and among ecosystems.
A **mass extinction** is a short geological interval in which species are lost far faster than they are replaced, worldwide.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think extinction is rare or recent?
cards.back: Most species that have ever lived are now **extinct**, and many vanished long before humans existed.
cards.hint: Consider how many species have existed in total.

cards.front: What happens to biodiversity in the millions of years after a mass extinction?
cards.back: Surviving groups evolve and spread into the **freed resources and space**, so diversity recovers over millions of years.

cards.front: Which causes have been proposed for mass extinctions?
cards.back: Huge **volcanic eruptions**, rapid climate change and an asteroid impact.
An **introduced species** is a species brought by human activity to an area where it did not naturally occur.

cards.front: Which species are most at risk of extinction?
cards.back: Species with **small ranges or narrow diets**, because a single change can remove all their food or living space.
cards.hint: Think about how many places and foods a species depends on.

cards.front: How are rocks dated so that fossils can be placed at a known time?
cards.back: Rocks are dated by the steady **decay of radioactive atoms**. Sedimentary layers normally have older rock beneath younger rock.
The **fossil record** is the collection of all known fossils, arranged by the age of the rock layers containing them.

cards.front: Why does a gap in the fossil record not prove a species was absent?
cards.back: The species may not have **fossilised**, or its fossils may simply not have been found yet.

cards.front: Why are soft-bodied organisms rarely preserved as fossils?
cards.back: They **decay quickly**, whereas shells and bones can last. Burial in sediment must also happen before the remains rot.
cards.hint: Compare soft tissue with hard parts.
